analysis.one_liner: Freezes large mergers among agribusiness, food processors, and grocery chains while a commission studies food-market concentration.
analysis.headline: Backed by 5 senators, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have temporarily banned large mergers among big agribusiness firms, food and beverage manufacturers, and grocery retailers — including companies like the four meatpackers that the bill says control 85% of beef processing. It also would have created a 12-member commission to study corporate concentration in the food system and recommend changes to antitrust law. The moratorium would have stayed in place until Congress passed comprehensive legislation addressing food-market concentration.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers would benefit from a pause on mergers among the large meatpackers, grain dealers, seed suppliers, and grocery retailers that buy their products, giving them more potential buyers and more bargaining power. Food and farm workers could gain from a required study of whether consolidation suppresses wages, and shoppers could gain if more competition eventually slowed grocery price increases. Rural communities dependent on family farms would benefit from slowed consolidation.

how_it_helps.text: Puts a moratorium on large mergers in the food chain — covering dealers, processors, brokers, agricultural input suppliers, and retailers above roughly $16-160 million in size — freezing consolidation while Congress considers structural fixes.

Creates a 12-member Food and Agriculture Concentration and Market Power Review Commission, required to include working farmers and a labor representative, to study concentration's effects on farmers' incomes, worker wages, rural communities, and grocery prices, and to recommend changes to antitrust law.

Documents in its findings that four beef packers now control 85% of that market, four pork packers 70%, and four infant formula makers nearly 90%, arguing this concentration leaves farmers with fewer buyers and shoppers paying more.

Keeps the moratorium in force until Congress passes comprehensive food-and-agriculture antitrust legislation, rather than letting it lapse on a fixed date, and lets the Attorney General waive it only in extraordinary circumstances such as a company's insolvency.

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness firms, food and beverage manufacturers, seed and chemical companies, and big grocery chains would pay, by being barred from merging with or acquiring each other until Congress passed replacement antitrust legislation. Any company that wanted to close an otherwise-legal deal would have to persuade the Attorney General that insolvency or similar financial distress justified a waiver.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is blunt and open-ended: it blocks most large mergers across the entire food sector with no set end date, until Congress enacts legislation declaring itself 'comprehensive,' which could take years or never happen.

The ban applies regardless of whether a specific merger would actually harm competition, so deals that could lower prices or save a struggling company would be frozen too; the only waiver is for 'extraordinary circumstances' like insolvency, giving the Attorney General wide, undefined discretion.
The size thresholds ($160 million for the larger firm, $16 million for the target) would sweep in mid-sized regional companies, not just the national giants the bill's findings describe.
The study commission is advisory only: it reports to Congress and the President with recommendations, and nothing in the bill requires any of them to be adopted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be a pause on further consolidation in a food system the bill itself documents as extraordinarily concentrated — four beef packers at 85%, four formula makers at nearly 90% — with a mandated study of how that concentration affects farmers, workers, and shoppers. The cost is real: a merger ban that is indifferent to whether each individual deal harms competition, with no sunset date and narrow waiver authority, could block efficiency-saving or rescue mergers and would depend entirely on Congress later passing the 'comprehensive legislation' that switches it off. A more targeted version tied to market-share tests would have carried less risk; as written, the tradeoff favors farmers and shoppers but at the price of a crude, potentially long-lasting freeze.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2022, by Sen. Cory Booker with Sens. Tester, Merkley, and Warren, and was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearings, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill was introduced against the backdrop of the 2022 infant formula shortage, which its findings cited as an example of the danger of four companies controlling nearly 90% of a market.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large agribusiness firms, meatpackers, seed and chemical companies, and big grocery chains are better off, because the merger moratorium never took effect and consolidation in the food system continued unchecked.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a moratorium on large food and agribusiness mergers and creating a study commission.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the merger moratorium bill, the only cosponsor from outside the Democratic Party.

against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action on it; it was never marked up, reported, or scheduled for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five sponsors were all Democrats or allied independents, no Republicans signed on, and no vote ever occurred, so partisan alignment is suggested but never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have barred companies with over $160 million in sales from merging with each other and blocked most acquisitions by large input suppliers like seed and fertilizer sellers. Its findings tie these companies' consolidation to quadrupling seed costs for farmers and to buyers pushing down farm prices.

Large seed, germplasm, and chemical sellers would have been covered by the merger ban; the bill cites three firms controlling two-thirds of world commodity seed and 70% of agrichemicals, and notes seed costs rose while the price farmers received barely did.

Retailers above the bill's size thresholds would have been barred from merging with or acquiring other large grocers. The bill's findings argue grocery prices rose three times faster than typical workers' earnings since the Great Recession while farmers' share of each retail dollar fell below 15 cents.

Food and beverage manufacturers above $160 million in sales would have been covered by the moratorium on mergers and acquisitions. Any planned deals would have been frozen until comprehensive antitrust legislation passed.
